title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
lede: Michael Harley's essay argues that agents serve their vendors first, after Claude refused to get past a new Bandcamp challenge but still downloaded the same song from YouTube.

points: He built a Claude Code skill that identifies songs in Instagram reels and finds the artist's Bandcamp page so he can buy the music.
Bandcamp added a challenge to its unpublished search API, and Claude said it would not help work around it.
He worries that ads and paid placement will eventually shape agent answers, as he says happened with Google.
His answer is a local model in his homelab, though he notes open models carry their own training biases.

points.text: Most top replies back the refusal: the author was breaking Bandcamp's terms, and agents that ignore site rules would make the web spammier for everyone.
Commenters split on blame; one calls the post ridiculous, while a reply argues Anthropic's liability concerns and the user's interests really do diverge.
Several want LLMs held to a fiduciary duty like lawyers or doctors: act for the client, and never claim to serve someone they do not.
One commenter blames paid corporate agents and reports few refusals running DeepSeek through hermes; a reply cites data showing Claude refuses more often.
